name: Diotimus of Miletus
bio: Diotimus of Miletus is one of the epigrammatists whose short poems were gathered in the Greek Anthology. Paton's index of authors dates the poet to 3rd century BC. Paton's index lists the poet among the writers of Meleager's Wreath, the Garland compiled about 100 BC.
This archive carries the 3 epigrams ascribed to the poet in the first volume of W. R. Paton's prose translation (Books I–VI) (Book V: 106; Book VI: 267, 358).

poems.title: Book V, 106
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: Granny, dear nurse, why do you bark at me when I approach, and cast me into torments twice as cruel. You accompany a lovely girl, and look how treading in her steps I go my own way, only gazing at her sweet form. Why be jealous of eyes, ill-fated nurse? We are allowed to look on the forms of even the immortals.

poems.title: Book VI, 267
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: Stand here, Artemis the Saviour, with thy torch on the land of Pollis, and give thy delightful light to him and to his children. The task is easy ; for no feeble knowledge hath he from Zeus of the unerring scales of Justice. And, Artemis, let the Graces too race over this grove, treading on the flowers with their light sandals.

poems.title: Book VI, 358
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: Hail, dainty frock, that Lydian Omphale doffed to goto the bed of Heracles. Thou wert blessed then, O frock, and blessed again art thou now that thou hast entered this golden house of Artemis.

poems.title: Book VII, 173
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.note: Attribution doubtful in Paton (Diotimus or Leonidas).
poems.text: Or themselves in the evening the kine came home to byre from the hill through the heavy snow. But Therimachus, alas sleeps the long sleep under the oak. The fire of heaven laid him to rest.

poems.title: Book VII, 227
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: Nor even a lion is as terrible in the mountains, as was Mico’s son Crinagoras in the clash of the shields. If this his covering be little, find no fault thereat; little is this land, but it bears men brave in war.

poems.title: Book VII, 261
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: What profiteth it to labour in childbirth and bring forth children if she who bears them is to see them dead! So his mother built the tomb for her little Bianor, while he should have done this for his mother.

poems.title: Book VII, 475
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: Scytuis the daughter of Polyaenus went to her father-in-law’s, lamenting, as she entered the wide gates, the death of her bridegroom, Evagoras the son of Hegemachus, who dwelt there. She came not back, poor widowed girl, to her father’s house, but within three months she perished, her spirit wasted by deadly melancholy. This tearful memorial of their love stands on the tomb of both beside the smooth high-way.

poems.title: Book VII, 733
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: We two old women Anaxo and Cleno the twin daughters of Epicrates were ever together; Cleno was in life the priestess of the Graces and Anaxo served Demeter. We wanted nine days to complete our eightieth year . . . We loved our husbands and children, and we, the old women, won gentle death before them.

poems.title: Book IX, 391
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.text: This son of Poseidon and the son of Zeus trained their youthful limbs for stubborn wrestling bouts. The contest is no brazen one for a caldron, but for which shall gain death or life. Antaeus has got the fall, and it was fit that Heracles, the son of Zeus, should win. Wrestling is Argive, not Libyan.

poems.title: On a Son, by His Mother (Mackail)
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: What profits it to labour in childbirth? what to bear children? let not her bear who must see her child's death: for to stripling Bianor his mother reared the tomb; but it was fitting that the mother should obtain this service of the son.

poems.title: Storm on the Hills (Mackail)
poems.author: Diotimus of Miletus
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Unherded at evenfall the oxen came to the farmyard from the hill, snowed on with heavy snow; alas, and Therimachus sleeps the long sleep beside an oak, stretched there by fire from heaven.
